analogy.p: Think of a playground where children are spread evenly between two sides of a see-saw. If extra children are added to the left side, children move across to the right so the see-saw rebalances: the system counteracts the change. Removing children from one side makes children move to that side. That maps onto Le Chatelier's principle for concentration changes: add reactant and the position shifts to the right, remove product and it shifts to the right. The analogy breaks down because real chemical changes are not people moving by choice; they happen because the forward and reverse rates change, and temperature and pressure effects have no simple equivalent on a see-saw.
analogy.t: A crowd on a see-saw playground

bullets: Statement to learn: 'If a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, then the system responds to counteract the change.'
'Counteract' means 'oppose' or 'work against', never 'help' or 'increase'.
The three changes you must be able to predict: concentration, temperature and (for gases) pressure.
A shift to the right gives more products at equilibrium; a shift to the left gives more reactants.
After the change the system is not at equilibrium for a short time; it then settles to a new equilibrium with new constant concentrations.
The principle gives the direction of change only; it does not tell you how big the change is.
Link to other topics: dynamic equilibrium (4.6.2), rates of reaction and collision theory, and the Haber process.
core.p: **Le Chatelier's principle** says that if a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, then the system responds to counteract the change. In other words, the position of equilibrium shifts so as to oppose whatever you did to it. This is a Higher tier idea. It does not explain why the shift happens (that comes from the rates of the forward and reverse reactions), but it lets you predict which way the position will move. You only need to apply it to changes in concentration, temperature and pressure for reversible reactions in a closed system.

bullets: Increase [reactant] → position shifts right (towards products), so more product is formed.
Decrease [product] (remove it) → position shifts right, so more reactants are used up and more product is formed.
Increase [product] → position shifts left (more reactants).
Decrease [reactant] → position shifts left.

Explanation in terms of rate: adding reactant increases the forward rate (more frequent collisions), so for a short time the forward rate is greater than the reverse rate until equilibrium is restored.
Industrial use: in the Haber process ammonia is removed by liquefying it, which shifts the equilibrium to the right so more ammonia is made.
On a concentration-time graph: when a reactant is added its line jumps up and then falls, while the product line rises, until both become horizontal at new values.
Link to other topics: concentration changes also affect rate (collision theory) but they change the position of equilibrium too.
core.p: If the concentration of a **reactant is increased**, the system responds by using up some of that extra reactant, so more products form until equilibrium is reached again. If the concentration of a **product is decreased** (for example by removing it), the system responds by making more of that product, so more reactants react to produce more products. In both cases the position of equilibrium shifts to the right. The reverse is also true: adding product, or removing reactant, shifts the position to the left.

bullets: Increase temperature → favours the endothermic direction (absorbs the extra heat).
Decrease temperature → favours the exothermic direction (releases heat to replace what was lost).
Forward exothermic (such as Haber, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol): increasing temperature shifts the position to the left, so less ammonia at equilibrium.
Forward endothermic (such as N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2, ΔH = +57 kJ/mol): increasing temperature shifts right, so more NO2 (a darker brown mixture).
The reverse reaction always has the opposite energy change, with the same size, so if the forward is exothermic the reverse is endothermic.
Always say 'relative amount of products' rather than just 'the yield goes up', and link it to exothermic or endothermic.
Temperature is the only one of the three changes that alters the numerical value of the equilibrium constant (not needed at GCSE), but it is also the only one that also changes the rate strongly.
Link to other topics: energy changes (4.5): you need to know whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic before predicting the shift.
core.p: The effect of temperature depends on whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is **increased**, the relative amount of products at equilibrium **increases for an endothermic reaction** and **decreases for an exothermic reaction**. If the temperature is **decreased**, the relative amount of products **decreases for an endothermic reaction** and **increases for an exothermic reaction**. The reason follows Le Chatelier: raising the temperature adds energy, so the system opposes this by favouring the direction that takes in energy (the endothermic direction); lowering the temperature favours the exothermic direction, which releases energy.

bullets: Count only gas molecules (gases, state symbol (g)) on each side of the balanced equation, using the big numbers in front.
Increase pressure → favours the side with fewer gas molecules; decrease pressure → favours the side with more gas molecules.
N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g): left side 1 + 3 = 4 molecules, right side 2 molecules; high pressure shifts the position right, giving more ammonia.
N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g): left side 1 molecule, right side 2 molecules; high pressure shifts the position left, so the mixture becomes lighter in colour.
If both sides have the same number of gas molecules, e.g. H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) (2 = 2), changing pressure has no effect on the position.
Solids and liquids are ignored when counting (their volume is tiny); in CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g) only the single CO2 counts, so high pressure favours the left.
Explain with the idea of pressure: the system reduces the pressure by reducing the number of gas particles.
Link to other topics: gas pressure and particle models (physics), and the cost of high-pressure industrial plant.
core.p: Pressure only affects the position of equilibrium for reactions in which **gases** are involved and the **number of molecules of gas is different on the two sides**. In a gas, pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls; more molecules in a given volume means higher pressure. If the pressure of a system at equilibrium is **increased**, the system responds by moving to the side that has the **smaller number of molecules** of gas (as shown by the balanced symbol equation), because that reduces the pressure. If the pressure is **decreased**, the position shifts towards the side with the **larger number of molecules** of gas.

bullets: Catalyst: speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally.
No change to the position of equilibrium or to the yield at equilibrium.
Equilibrium is reached sooner (it saves time and so saves money).
Catalysts provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
In the Haber process an iron catalyst lets the reaction go fast enough at a moderate temperature (about 450 °C).
On a graph the plateau stays at the same height; only the time to reach it is shorter.
Note: this is not an example of Le Chatelier's principle, because the catalyst is not changing a condition that the system can oppose.
Link to other topics: rates of reaction (4.6.1) and catalysts in industry.
core.p: A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium. It increases the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction by the same amount, because it lowers the activation energy for both directions equally. The result is that equilibrium is reached more quickly, but the relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium are exactly the same as without the catalyst. This is a favourite exam point because many students think a catalyst gives a better yield.

bullets: Change at equilibrium → forward and reverse rates become unequal.
The faster reaction continues until the rates are equal again (new equilibrium).
Add reactant: forward rate increases first, so net shift right, then reverse rate rises until equal.
Increase temperature: both rates increase, but the endothermic direction increases by more, so the position shifts in the endothermic direction.
Increase pressure: gas concentrations increase, and the side with more molecules is affected more, so net shift towards the side with fewer molecules.
Catalyst: both rates increase equally, so they stay equal and there is no shift.
Use phrases such as 'the rate of the forward reaction becomes greater than the rate of the reverse reaction'.
Link to other topics: collision theory (frequency of collisions and activation energy).
core.h: Explaining shifts in terms of rates
core.p: Le Chatelier tells you what will happen; collision theory explains why. When you change a condition at equilibrium, the forward and reverse rates are no longer equal for a short time. The reaction with the higher rate dominates until the amounts change enough for the rates to become equal again. For example, adding reactant raises the forward rate immediately (more reactant particles, more frequent collisions), so more product is made, which in turn increases the reverse rate until both are equal once more at a new equilibrium. Using this reasoning gets extra marks in 'explain' questions.

bullets: Pressure: high pressure favours the right (4 → 2 molecules), but very high pressure needs strong, expensive equipment and more energy, so 200 atm is a compromise.
Temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give more ammonia at equilibrium, but the rate would be too slow, so about 450 °C is used.
Catalyst (iron): speeds up the reaction so equilibrium is reached quickly; it does not change the yield at equilibrium.
Removing ammonia by cooling and liquefying it shifts the position to the right, so more ammonia forms.
Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back into the reactor.
Only about 15 to 30 per cent of the gases are converted in one pass; recycling means a high overall conversion.
Raw materials: nitrogen from the air, hydrogen from natural gas.
Link to other topics: Haber process and NPK fertilisers in 'Using resources' (4.10).
core.h: Applying the principle: the Haber process
core.p: The Haber process is the standard application. The reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) has a forward reaction that is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol) and has 4 gas molecules on the left but only 2 on the right. Le Chatelier's principle says low temperature and high pressure would give the highest yield of ammonia. In practice the conditions used are a **compromise**: about 450 °C, 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst, because a low temperature makes the rate too slow, and very high pressure is very expensive and dangerous to maintain.

bullets: Low temperature: better yield for an exothermic reaction, but slower rate; high temperature gives a faster rate but a lower yield, so a compromise temperature is used.
High pressure: better yield (when fewer gas molecules on the product side) and faster rate (more frequent collisions), but expensive and hazardous.
Catalyst: faster rate at lower temperature, reducing energy costs, with no change in yield.
Recycling unreacted reactants saves raw materials and increases overall yield.
Removal of product shifts position to the right but may require extra equipment or cooling.
A good evaluation mentions both advantages and disadvantages and gives a conclusion.
Sustainable development: reducing energy use lowers cost and pollution.
Link to other topics: percentage yield and atom economy (4.3).
core.h: A compromise between yield, rate and cost
core.p: In industry, the best conditions are not simply those that give the highest yield. Chemists must balance **yield** (the amount of product at equilibrium), **rate** (how fast the product is made) and **cost** (energy, equipment, safety). A condition that favours the position of equilibrium may slow the reaction, or be too expensive to maintain. This idea is often examined by asking you to 'evaluate' or 'justify' conditions, so you should link each condition to its effect on both position and rate.

bullets: Step 1: write the equation with ⇌ and the state symbols.
Step 2: note whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic (for temperature) and count gas molecules on each side (for pressure).
Step 3: state the change (for example 'pressure is increased').
Step 4: say how the system opposes it ('moves to the side with fewer gas molecules').
Step 5: give the result ('position shifts to the right, so more ammonia').
Step 6: if asked, link to the rate or to colour change.
Never write 'the reaction goes faster to the right'; write 'the position of equilibrium shifts to the right'.
Check that you did not forget the catalyst case (no effect on position).
core.h: A step-by-step method for predicting a shift
core.p: Examiners reward a clear method, so follow the same steps every time. First write out the balanced equation and note the state of each substance. Next identify the type of change (concentration, temperature or pressure). Then decide what the system must do to oppose that change. Finally state the direction of the shift and what that means for the amount of product, and finish with the reason. Practising this routine on several reactions will let you answer quickly and accurately in the exam.

bullets: If a reactant is added: its line steps up at that moment, then falls; the product line rises; both level out at new values.
If a product is removed: its line steps down, then rises; the reactant line falls.
Temperature or pressure change: lines curve smoothly to new horizontal levels (no vertical step) because the amounts do not change instantly.
New plateau higher for products than before means the position has shifted right.
Colour clues: darker brown for N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 means more NO2 (position right); lighter means more N2O4 (position left).
A larger gap between plateau levels indicates a bigger shift.
State the evidence: 'the concentration of B increases from 0.60 to 0.84 mol/dm3'.
Link to other topics: graph skills in maths, reading values accurately.
core.h: Interpreting graphs and data after a change
core.p: After a change is made to an equilibrium mixture, the graph of concentration against time shows a sudden step (if a concentration was altered) or a gradual change in slope, followed by a new horizontal section. Learning to read these graphs is a data skill that is often tested. Look for which line jumps, which line then moves in the opposite direction, and what the final levels are compared with the original levels. Temperature and pressure changes do not cause jumps in the amounts at the instant of change; the amounts move smoothly to new constant values.

bullets: **Link 1:** name the change (concentration, temperature or pressure) and whether it increased or decreased.
**Link 2:** say the system responds to oppose the change, so the equilibrium position shifts.
**Link 3:** give the direction (left or right, towards reactants or products) with a reason: fewer gas molecules, endothermic direction, or using up the added substance.
**Link 4:** state the result: the yield of product at equilibrium increases or decreases.
**Rate separate:** a higher temperature or pressure also increases the rate of both reactions, so equilibrium is reached sooner.
**Never write** that the reaction 'stops' or that the catalyst shifts the position.
core.h: Writing a Higher-tier explanation of a shift
core.p: AQA expects Higher tier answers about equilibrium to follow a clear chain of reasoning, and marks are earned for each link in the chain. First state the change that was made to the system, for example that the pressure is increased or the temperature is lowered. Second, state that the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change, in the direction that counteracts it. Third, identify the direction and the consequence, naming which side is favoured and what happens to the amount of product at equilibrium. Finally, if the question asks about rate or cost, comment separately on the rate, because a change in the position of equilibrium and a change in the rate are different ideas.

bullets: **Count gases only:** ignore solids and liquids when comparing molecules.
**Equal moles:** if both sides have the same number of gas molecules, pressure has no effect on the position.
**Exothermic forward:** a higher temperature shifts left and a lower temperature shifts right.
**Endothermic forward:** a higher temperature shifts right and a lower temperature shifts left.
**Reverse is opposite:** the energy change of the reverse reaction has the same size but the opposite sign.
**Catalyst:** no shift, since it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally.
core.h: Quick checks: counting gas molecules and the heat direction
core.p: Two quick checks let you predict almost any shift in the Higher specification. For pressure, count only the gaseous molecules on each side of the balanced equation using the big numbers in front of each formula; for N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 that is 4 on the left and 2 on the right, so higher pressure favours the right. For temperature, look at the sign of the energy change for the forward reaction: if it is exothermic (negative) the reverse is endothermic, and raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction. If the number of gas molecules is the same on both sides, such as in H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI, changing the pressure does not change the position of equilibrium.

exam: Learn the statement of Le Chatelier's principle word for word: 'if a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, then the system responds to counteract the change'.

For a 'predict' question (1 mark) give the direction: 'shifts to the right / more product'. For 'explain' (2 to 3 marks) add the reason: 'because the forward reaction is endothermic' or 'because there are fewer gas molecules on the right'.
Temperature answers need three parts: the direction of the shift, whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and the effect on the amount of product.
Pressure answers need the count of gas molecules on each side, for example '4 molecules on the left, 2 on the right', and the conclusion 'favours the side with fewer molecules'.
If the number of gas molecules is equal on both sides, state clearly that a change in pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium.
Catalyst answer for full marks: no effect on the position; both rates increase equally; equilibrium is reached more quickly.
For 4 mark industrial conditions questions, link each condition (temperature, pressure, catalyst, removal of product) to yield and to rate, and mention cost.
For 6 mark 'evaluate' questions, give conditions that favour yield, conditions that favour rate, the compromise chosen, and a justified conclusion.
Say 'position of equilibrium' not 'the reaction'; say 'shifts', 'moves' or 'favours' for the direction.
Graph questions: describe jumps and plateaus using numbers with units, and decide which direction the position moved.
Colour questions: relate the observation to the species, for example N2O4 colourless and NO2 brown, so a darker brown means more NO2.
Check that you quote the correct sign of the enthalpy change; the reverse reaction has the opposite sign.

mistakes.r: A catalyst speeds up both directions equally; equilibrium is reached faster but the position is unchanged.
mistakes.w: A catalyst moves the equilibrium to the right so more product is made.

mistakes.r: It increases the yield only if the forward reaction is endothermic; for an exothermic forward reaction the yield falls.
mistakes.w: Increasing the temperature always increases the yield.

mistakes.r: It moves to the side with fewer gas molecules; count the gas molecules in the balanced equation.
mistakes.w: Increasing pressure always moves equilibrium to the right.

mistakes.r: If the numbers of gas molecules are equal on both sides, pressure has no effect on the position.
mistakes.w: Pressure has an effect when there are the same number of gas molecules on both sides.

mistakes.r: Only gases are counted; solids and liquids are ignored.
mistakes.w: Count all the substances, including solids, when working out the effect of pressure.

mistakes.r: The system counteracts the change, working against it (adding reactant, so it uses up reactant).
mistakes.w: The system opposes the change by making the change bigger.

mistakes.r: Say 'the position of equilibrium shifts to the right'; do not describe the speed of one direction in isolation.
mistakes.w: The reaction goes faster to the right so the equilibrium moves.

mistakes.r: 450 °C is a compromise: a lower temperature would give a higher yield but the rate would be too slow.
mistakes.w: The Haber process uses 450 °C because that gives the highest yield.

summary: Higher tier: Le Chatelier's principle states that if a system at equilibrium has a condition changed, the system responds to counteract the change. You must predict how the position of equilibrium shifts when concentration, temperature or pressure (for gases) is changed, and explain industrial compromises such as the Haber process.

terms.d: If a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, then the system responds to counteract the change.
The relative amounts of reactants and products in the equilibrium mixture.
The position of equilibrium moves so that more products (and fewer reactants) are present.
The position of equilibrium moves so that more reactants (and fewer products) are present.
In a closed system, forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings.
A system in which no reactants or products can escape.
The amount of product obtained compared with the maximum possible amount.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up; it does not change the position of equilibrium.
A balanced symbol equation, whose big numbers give the number of molecules (moles) of each substance.
Conditions chosen to balance yield, rate and cost in an industrial process.
The industrial manufacture of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g).
Returning unreacted reactants to the reactor so they can react again.

worked.ans: (a) Darker brown, because increasing the temperature shifts the position towards the endothermic (forward) direction, forming more NO2. (b) Paler, because increasing the pressure shifts the position to the side with fewer gas molecules (1 molecule of N2O4 on the left rather than 2 of NO2), so more colourless N2O4 forms.
worked.q: The reaction N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g) is endothermic in the forward direction. N2O4 is colourless and NO2 is brown. A sealed syringe containing the equilibrium mixture is (a) heated, and then (b) the pressure is increased. Predict and explain the colour change in each case. (4 marks)
steps: (a) Forward reaction is endothermic, so raising the temperature favours the forward direction.
The position shifts to the right and more NO2 forms, so the mixture becomes darker brown.
Increasing the pressure favours the side with fewer molecules, which is the left, so the position shifts towards N2O4 and the mixture becomes paler.

worked.ans: High pressure, because there are 3 gas molecules on the left and only 1 on the right, so increasing the pressure shifts the position to the right. Low temperature, because the forward reaction is exothermic, so decreasing the temperature shifts the position to the right, giving more methanol.
worked.q: The reaction CO(g) + 2H2(g) ⇌ CH3OH(g) is exothermic in the forward direction. State and explain the conditions of temperature and pressure that would give the highest equilibrium yield of methanol. (4 marks)
steps: High pressure favours the side with fewer molecules, so the position shifts right and more methanol forms.
Forward reaction exothermic: a low temperature favours the exothermic direction.
So the position shifts right and more methanol forms at low temperature.

worked.ans: 450 °C is a compromise between a high yield, which needs a low temperature because the forward reaction is exothermic, and a fast rate, which needs a high temperature. The iron catalyst increases the rate of both reactions equally so equilibrium is reached quickly at this temperature, but it does not change the yield.
worked.q: In the Haber process N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol), the temperature used is about 450 °C. Explain why this is a compromise and why a catalyst is used. (4 marks)
steps: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would shift the position to the right, giving a higher yield.
But a lower temperature makes the rate too slow.
A higher temperature gives a faster rate but a lower equilibrium yield, so 450 °C balances yield and rate.
A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster without changing the position.
